title: The two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28)
hookLine: the true mother gives up her claim to save the child

cards: Two women stand before the king, and there is one baby. They live in the same house, and nobody else was there. Each had a son, a few days apart.
In the night one baby died, and now each woman says the living child is hers. No witnesses, no records, no way to check. One says, she switched them while I slept.
The other says, no, the dead one is yours, the living one is mine. Back and forth, in front of the throne.
And the new king, the one who asked for a listening heart, says something that silences the room: bring me a sword.

teach.b: The text calls the two women harlots and never gives their names. They come with no one to speak for them, and the king hears them anyway, in person. First Solomon says both claims back, exactly.

teach.h: DIVIDE THE LIVING CHILD IN TWO.
teach.b: Then the sword, and the order: divide the living child in two, half to the one and half to the other. Here's the turn.

teach.h: GIVE HER THE CHILD. DON'T KILL HIM.
teach.b: One woman cries out: give her the living child, and don't kill him. The text says she spoke because her compassion was stirred for her son; the Hebrew word is rachamim.
The other says, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "It shall be neither mine nor thine; divide it." And the king answers: give the first woman the living child. She is his mother.
He didn't find new evidence. He made a moment where love would have to show itself, and it did, as giving way.

The real mother was willing to lose the case to save the child. Then the text adds a line about everyone else: all Israel heard of the judgment, and saw that the wisdom of God was in the king, to do justice.

teach.h: IT SHALL BE NEITHER MINE NOR THINE.
teach.b: Inside the clever lesson sits a hard one. Sometimes the person who is right is the one willing to stop fighting. She didn't win by arguing better.
And Solomon's listening heart heard the difference between someone who wanted the child and someone who only wanted to win.

how: Jews read the judgment of Solomon in the book of Kings, and the passage is assigned as the haftarah, the reading from the Prophets, for the Torah portion Miketz.

o: a mother's anger when her child is threatened
the sorrow of losing a child in the night
compassion, a deep and tender love that moves you

games.q: the real mother gives way — tap the pairs.
p: what Israel saw in the king

s: Solomon found the mother by questioning witnesses
there were no witnesses. he called for a sword and watched who would give way.
the text gives the two women's names
they are never named. the text calls them harlots, and the king hears them anyway.
the real mother asked for the child to be given to the other woman
she would rather lose him than see him die.

games.q: you're the real mother. the king has ordered the child cut in two, half to each woman. what do you say?
o: beg the king to give him to the other woman.
agree, since the king has spoken.
games.why: she cried out to give the child to the other woman and not to kill him, and that is how Solomon knew she was his mother.

practice: Pick a disagreement you're in right now, a family argument, a fight over credit at work, and ask what's actually at stake underneath: a relationship, a child's peace, a friendship.
Hold the two side by side, the win and the child, without deciding anything yet. If you pray, you can ask for the heart to know the difference.

wordCard.voice: Rachamim. The compassion that stirred in the real mother when the sword was raised over her child. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: compassion. the real mother's rachamim was stirred for her son.

carryVoice: Your line: the real mother gives way. Her love showed itself by letting go. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: It shall be neither mine nor thine; divide it.
